Acousmatic music is a genre of electroacoustic music that is composed for playback via speakers, rather than being performed live by musicians with visible instruments. The listener engages with the pure sonic experience, unmediated by the visual cues of instrumental performance.
I use this term to refer to when I have a true musical experience. It applies to both making and listening to music.
Describes a scale with no semitones between adjacent steps. From the Greek an- ("without") and hēmitonion ("half tone").
The opposite is hemitonic: a scale with one or more semitone steps.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Anhemitonic: Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major and its modes, including Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Hemitonic: Music/Scale/Hirajoshi and the other Japanese in-scale pentatonics.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Music/Scale/Whole Tone is also anhemitonic. Every seven-note scale in twelve-tone equal temperament is hemitonic.

Bariolage is a string playing technique, primarily used on the Violin (but also on other bowed string instruments), characterized by rapid alternation between notes on adjacent strings—often between a static open string and varying stopped notes on a neighboring string.
Creates a shimmering or pulsating texture.
Common in Baroque and Classical music, notably in J.S. Bach’s solo string works.
Exploits the contrast in tone between open and fingered strings.
Often used to simulate polyphony or to add rhythmic drive.
In Bach’s Partita No. 3 in E major, BWV 1006, the Preludio uses bariolage extensively, alternating between the open E string and notes played on the A string.
From French barioler, meaning "to streak with several colors"—a metaphor for the tonal contrasts produced.

Scientific pitch notation names a pitch with a letter and an octave number: C4, G1, F♯5. The letter names the note, and the number says which octave of the whole audible range it sits in.
Middle C is C4, about 261.63 Hz. The A above it, A4, is the 440 Hz tuning note.
It is also called American standard pitch notation (ASPN) and international pitch notation (IPN).
The number goes up by one at each C. B3 is the note just below C4, and every note from C4 up through B4 carries the 4.
Each octave doubles the frequency: C3 is about 130.81 Hz, C4 about 261.63 Hz, C5 about 523.25 Hz.
An 88-key piano runs from A0 (27.5 Hz) to C8 (about 4186 Hz).
So a "low G" can be any of several notes. G1 (49 Hz) is a deep bass note near the bottom of a bass guitar's range; G3 (196 Hz) sits just below middle C.
MIDI sends a note as a number from 0 to 127 and leaves naming to the software. In scientific pitch notation, note 60 is C4, note 69 is A4, note 0 is C−1 and note 127 is G9.
Note number = 12 × (octave + 1) + semitones above C. G1 is 12 × 2 + 7 = 31, and F1 is 12 × 2 + 5 = 29.
The frequency of note m at A440 tuning is 440 × 2^((m − 69) / 12) Hz.
A note number carries no sharp or flat spelling. MIDI note 34 is both A♯1 and B♭1; the musical key decides which name to write.
